code.title: Core functional interfaces in action

followUps:
Yes, a functional interface can extend another interface, as long as the result still has exactly one abstract method in total.

The child may add default or static methods, or re-declare an inherited abstract method. Example: interface Pred2<T> extends Predicate<T> { default Pred2<T> not() { return x -> !test(x); } } is still functional because only test is abstract. If the child added a second abstract method, a lambda could not implement it and @FunctionalInterface would give a compile error.

They exist to avoid boxing, which means wrapping an int into an Integer object.

A Predicate<Integer> forces every int through an Integer allocation (values outside -128..127 are new objects), while IntPredicate takes a plain int. Over 1,000,000 elements that means up to 1,000,000 fewer small objects for the garbage collector. Generics cannot use primitives, so Java ships hand-written variants: IntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntUnaryOperator, IntSupplier and the Long and Double families.

code.title: Lambda this vs anonymous class this

followUps:
Choose an anonymous class when you need more than a single-method lambda can give: state, several methods, or a class that is not an interface.

Typical cases: extending an abstract class (such as TimerTask), implementing an interface with more than one abstract method (a listener with 3 callbacks), keeping a field like a counter between calls, or needing this to mean the object itself (to unregister a listener from inside it). Also, a lambda has no name in stack traces, so a named class is sometimes easier to debug.

invokedynamic lets the JVM decide how to build the lambda object at run time (the first time the line runs) instead of baking one fixed class into the compiled code.

The compiler only emits a private method and a call site. On first execution, LambdaMetafactory generates the implementing class in memory and links it. Benefits: no extra Outer$1.class files on disk, smaller jars, faster startup for many lambdas, and freedom for future JVMs to change the strategy (for example caching non-capturing lambdas as one shared instance) without recompiling your code.

code.title: Captured locals and workarounds

followUps:
Not always: the variable (the reference) is safe because it never changes, but the object it points to can still be changed by anyone.

If you capture a List<String> list that is effectively final, the lambda still sees the same list, and calling list.add(x) from several threads without synchronisation can lose updates or throw ConcurrentModificationException. Example: 1,000 parallel tasks each adding 1 item to an ArrayList may end with 987 items. Use a concurrent collection, collect, or immutable data to make it safe.

Anonymous classes had the same rule: before Java 8 a captured local had to be declared final, and since Java 8 effectively final is enough.

The reason is identical: the compiler copies the local's value into a hidden field of the anonymous object (a synthetic val$x field set in its constructor). A later change to the original local would not reach that copy. The anonymous class can still keep its own mutable fields, which is the standard way to hold changing state: new Runnable() { int count; public void run() { count++; } }.

code.title: The four method reference kinds

followUps:
It is ambiguous because Integer has two toString methods that both fit the shape Function<Integer,String>.

The static Integer.toString(int i) matches as i -> Integer.toString(i). The instance toString() matches as i -> i.toString() (unbound receiver). The compiler cannot pick one and reports an error. Fix it by writing a lambda, String::valueOf, or Object::toString.

Because this::onEvent creates a new lambda object each time it is written, so the object you pass to remove is not equal to the one you added.

bus.add(this::onEvent);
bus.remove(this::onEvent); // different object, nothing removed

Lambdas and method references have identity equality, and two evaluations of the same expression are not guaranteed to be the same instance. Store the reference in a field: Listener l = this::onEvent; bus.add(l); bus.remove(l);. The listener then stays registered correctly and cannot leak.

code.title: Streams are lazy until a terminal op

followUps:
Stateful intermediate operations are the ones that must remember earlier elements: sorted, distinct, limit, skip and (in practice) takeWhile/dropWhile in ordered streams.

sorted buffers all N elements (O(N) memory) before passing any on. distinct keeps a set of seen values. limit(5) and skip(5) keep a counter. Stateless ones (filter, map, flatMap, peek, mapToInt) handle each element alone, which is why they split easily across threads.

Because count() can sometimes compute the answer without running the pipeline, so peek never gets called.

Since Java 9, if the source has a known size and no stage changes it (only map, peek, sorted), count() returns that size directly. Stream.of(1,2,3).peek(print).count() prints nothing and returns 3. Add a filter and the size is unknown, so the elements are traversed and peek prints 3 lines. Never rely on peek for needed side effects.

code.title: Execution order and the sorted barrier

followUps:
It sets a flag that tells the source to stop pulling more elements once the limit has been reached.

Each stage in the pipeline is a sink. limit(n) counts the elements it accepts, and when the count hits n its cancellationRequested() returns true. The source loop (for example the spliterator's forEachRemaining replaced by a tryAdvance loop) checks that flag before each next element. With limit(2) on an infinite iterate, only 2 elements are produced, then the loop ends.

With parallel() the source is split into chunks that run on several threads, so the order of the lambda calls is no longer the order of the data.

For findFirst on 4 elements, different threads may run filter on 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the same time, so extra work happens, but the result must still be the first match in encounter order (20). Short-circuiting needs coordination between threads, and printing inside lambdas shows an unpredictable order. Use findAny or unordered() if order does not matter.

code.title: map vs flatMap, also on Optional

followUps:
When a stage returns an empty stream, flatMap simply contributes nothing to the result, so that element disappears.

Example: orders [pen, ink], [], [book] flatMapped with o -> o.items().stream() gives [pen, ink, book]: 3 items from 3 orders, the empty one adds zero. That is why flatMap(x -> opt(x).stream()) works as a combined map and filter. A null returned from the function (instead of an empty stream) is treated as empty too.

mapMulti is better when each element produces only a few results (0 to 3), because it avoids creating a small stream object for every element.

Stream.of(1,2,3).<Integer>mapMulti((x, sink) -> {
    sink.accept(x); sink.accept(x * 10);
})  // 1,10,2,20,3,30

The lambda pushes results into a consumer, so there is less allocation. It is also handy for conditional logic that is awkward as a stream. For large or already-stream-shaped inner data (a whole list per element), plain flatMap is clearer and just as fast.

code.title: groupingBy with downstream collectors

followUps:
Use collectingAndThen to wrap maxBy and unwrap its Optional with Optional::get.

Map<String, Emp> top = emps.stream().collect(
  groupingBy(Emp::dept, collectingAndThen(
    maxBy(comparingInt(Emp::salary)), Optional::get)));

Calling get is safe because a group exists only if it has at least one element, so the maxBy result is never empty. Alternative: toMap(Emp::dept, identity(), BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparingInt(Emp::salary))), which merges duplicate keys directly and gives plain values. With 5 employees in 3 departments you get 3 entries.

groupingByConcurrent collects into one shared ConcurrentHashMap from many threads, while groupingBy builds a separate map per thread and merges them.

The concurrent version can be faster on large parallel streams because there is no merge step, but the order of elements inside each group is not guaranteed and it only helps when the stream is parallel and the downstream collector is thread-safe. For sequential streams, or when you need encounter order inside groups, use plain groupingBy. It also returns a ConcurrentMap.

code.title: reduce vs collect

followUps:
Create it with Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher). Example: join numbers with a plus sign.

Collector<Integer, StringJoiner, String> c = Collector.of(
  () -> new StringJoiner("+"),
  (j, n) -> j.add(String.valueOf(n)),
  StringJoiner::merge, StringJoiner::toString);

Supplier makes an empty container, accumulator adds one element, combiner merges two containers (used in parallel runs), finisher converts to the final result. Input 1,2,3 gives 1+2+3. Time is O(n).

They are hints that let the stream library skip work or reorder it safely.

  • IDENTITY_FINISH: the container already is the result, so the finisher is skipped (like toList()).
  • UNORDERED: the result does not depend on element order, so a parallel run may combine in any order.
  • CONCURRENT: many threads may add to one shared container at the same time, so no per-thread containers or combining are needed; the container must be thread-safe.

Wrong flags give wrong results, so set them only if true.

code.title: Parallel stream pitfalls and fixes

followUps:
Submit the whole terminal operation from inside your own ForkJoinPool, and the stream uses that pool's threads instead of the common pool.

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
long r = pool.submit(() ->
   LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 1000).parallel().sum()).get();
pool.shutdown();

This works because the parallel tasks fork into the pool of the thread that started them. It is an implementation behavior rather than a documented guarantee, so test it. Always shut the pool down. It stops blocking work from starving the shared common pool.

No: they solve different problems. Virtual threads help with many waiting (I/O) tasks, parallel streams help with CPU-heavy data crunching.

A virtual thread is cheap, so you can run 100,000 blocking HTTP calls at once, but it does not add CPU cores. A parallel stream splits one CPU-bound job over about as many threads as cores (8 cores gives at most about 8x). For CPU-bound work virtual threads give no speedup. For I/O fan-out, use virtual threads (an executor per task) and not parallel streams.

code.title: orElse vs orElseGet vs orElseThrow

followUps:
or() returns another Optional when the first one is empty, so you can chain fallbacks without leaving Optional.

Optional<User> u = cache.find(id)
    .or(() -> db.find(id))
    .or(() -> remote.find(id));

Each supplier runs lazily only if everything before it was empty. orElse and orElseGet return a bare value instead, which ends the chain. Before Java 9 you needed an isPresent ladder or map tricks.

Yes, but only at the edge where you hand a value to old code that expects null, such as a legacy API, a JSON mapper or a database parameter.

Example: statement.setString(1, name.orElse(null)). Inside your own logic, avoid it, because it throws away the whole point of Optional and brings the null checks back. Compared with orElse(""), null needs the receiver to handle it. If you find yourself writing orElse(null) then calling a method on it, use map instead.

code.title: Optional best practices in a chain

followUps:
Add the Optional version next to the old one, mark the old one deprecated, and move callers over gradually.

Steps: 1) add Optional<String> findName() (or a new name) implemented as Optional.ofNullable(getName()); 2) annotate the old getName() with @Deprecated and document that it can return null; 3) migrate callers module by module; 4) remove the old method in a later major version. A rename is needed because Java cannot overload on return type alone. Never change the old signature in place, since that breaks every caller at once.

Annotations such as JSpecify's @Nullable cover the places Optional should not be used: fields, parameters and generic type arguments.

Optional is best for return values that may be absent, so callers are forced to handle it. Annotations document intent for fields (@Nullable String middleName) and parameters, and tools like NullAway or the IDE warn about unsafe dereferences at compile time with no extra object. Together: Optional for results, annotations for everything else, and non-null by default.

code.title: Stateful vs stateless operations

followUps:
The stream reads limit as a cap on what comes after sorted, but sorted still has to see all elements first.

Example: Stream.of(5,3,8,1).sorted().limit(2) reads all 4 elements, sorts to 1,3,5,8, then passes only 1 and 3. The JDK may use a bounded approach in some cases, but you should assume O(N log N) time and O(N) memory. If you only need the 2 smallest of a huge input, a heap of size 2 is O(N log 2), which is far cheaper than a full sort.

When the source is already sorted or already distinct, the stream library knows it and can skip the work.

Streams carry flags: SORTED and DISTINCT. A TreeSet stream has SORTED (and DISTINCT), so sorted() with the natural order does nothing. A Set from HashSet has DISTINCT, so distinct() is a no-op. sorted() followed by distinct() can then use cheap neighbour comparison. A map clears these flags because values change.

code.title: Checked exceptions inside stream lambdas

followUps:
Collect failures as data: return a small result record per element, then split successes and failures with partitioningBy.

record R(String in, Integer val, String err) {}
Map<Boolean, List<R>> parts = results.stream()
  .collect(partitioningBy(r -> r.err() == null));

For inputs 1, bad, 3 the true list has 2 values and the false list has 1 error message. Nothing is lost and no exception aborts the pipeline. Same idea works with an Either or Try type.

It exists so you can carry an IOException through code that cannot declare checked exceptions, such as a lambda, without losing the original error.

It is a runtime exception that wraps an IOException and keeps it as the cause, so the caller can unwrap it with e.getCause() and handle I/O errors properly. The JDK uses it itself, for example in Files.lines iteration and BufferedReader.lines(). A plain RuntimeException would work, but this type says exactly what went wrong.

code.title: Loop vs IntStream vs boxed Stream

followUps:
A megamorphic call site is a single line of code that, at run time, calls many different implementations (usually more than 2).

The JIT compiler speeds up calls by guessing the target and inlining it. With 1 type (monomorphic) or 2 (bimorphic) it inlines, but with 3 or more it falls back to a slow virtual call through a table. In streams, the shared map sink calls whichever lambda you gave it, so a utility used with 5 different lambdas can become megamorphic, which hurts hot loops. Keep hot pipelines using few distinct lambdas.

Escape analysis can remove the Optional or lambda object entirely when the JIT proves it never leaves the method, but it is not guaranteed.

If findUser(id).map(...).orElse(x) is fully inlined, the Optional is created and discarded in the same compiled method, so the JIT can replace it with plain local variables (scalar replacement) and allocate nothing. If the call is too big to inline, or the Optional is stored or returned beyond the inlined area, it is allocated on the heap. Measure with JFR allocation profiling, and do not avoid Optional only from fear of this cost.
